Couples

Jealousy: when does it stop being normal?

Feeling jealous now and then is human. Controlling, monitoring or isolating a partner is not.

Seeing your partner chatting animatedly with someone attractive and feeling a pang of unease is a common experience. Jealousy is an emotion that arises when we feel a valued relationship is under threat.

An emotion with several faces

Researchers distinguish between emotional jealousy, the feeling of insecurity or distress that most people experience at some point, and cognitive and behavioural jealousy: persistent suspicious thoughts and behaviours such as checking a partner's phone, tracking their movements or interrogating them. The latter are linked with poorer relationship quality.

Jealousy increases with personal insecurity, past experiences of infidelity or abandonment, and dependence. Sometimes it responds to real signs; at other times to exaggerated interpretations.

A red line

The myth that "jealousy is proof of love" is dangerous. When jealousy turns into control, prohibitions, surveillance or isolation from friends and family, we are not talking about love but about an abusive relationship. This pattern is one of the early signs of intimate partner violence.

What usually helps

  • Talk about the discomfort without accusing: "I felt insecure when…" rather than "you always…".
  • Separate facts from assumptions.
  • Work on your own insecurity, which is not solved by watching the other person.
  • Seek professional help if jealousy keeps recurring and harming the relationship.
If your partner controls you, isolates you or frightens you, seek help. In Spain you can call 016, free of charge and not shown on the phone bill.

References

  1. Pfeiffer, S. M. y Wong, P. T. P. (1989). Multidimensional jealousy. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 6(2), 181–196.
  2. Buss, D. M. (2000). The Dangerous Passion. Free Press.
  3. Ministerio de Igualdad. 016, servicio de atención a víctimas de violencia de género.
